clue.text: Like Rodin's'model describing a small red 'book

definitions.text: Like Rodin's'model describing a small red 'book

parts.words: Like Rodin's'model describing a small red 'book
parts.note: Rodin's sculpture The Thinker sits lost in meditation, and a little book of reflections could carry the same adjective

explanation.surface: An art-lover pictures a sculptor's sitter reading out of a little red volume.
explanation.walkthrough: Rodin's famous statue is The Thinker, chin on hand; the adjective that fits him also describes a slim book full of musings.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone deep in meditation, like the sculpted figure, is pensive and reflective.

clue.text: Come here and, cries Aunt Sally's barker

definitions.text: Come here and, cries Aunt Sally's barker

parts.words: Come here and, cries Aunt Sally's barker
parts.note: the fairground showman invites people to step up and throw at the dummy woman; his call 'come' plus the missing word also reads as an old phrase for come here

explanation.surface: A fairground stallholder calls out to passers-by to try their luck.
explanation.walkthrough: Aunt Sally is a British fairground game where players throw sticks at a wooden figure of a woman; the barker urges you to hit her, which also gives 'come hither'.
explanation.definitionFit: The old word for 'to this place' completes 'come ...', and it sounds like an invitation to strike the woman.

clue.text: Some go up a street, dying to get in its shade

definitions.text: dying to get in its shade

indicators.note: some means only part of the following words is used, the answer running across them

explanation.surface: A few people walk up a road, longing to reach the shade of its trees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dying to get in' sounds like eagerness, but the Javanese upas tree was fabled to kill anyone resting in its shade; 'Some' signals the run inside GO UP A STREET.
explanation.definitionFit: The upas tree of Java was fabled to poison everything beneath it, so lying in its shade meant death; the phrase also means in a fix.

clue.text: Skill of worker in charge of floating logs

parts.note: a hand is a manual worker, as in farmhand
a raft is a platform of logs lashed together to float

explanation.surface: A labourer is responsible for logs drifting down a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skill' here means a craft practised by hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Manual skill in making decorative objects is a craft worked by hand, such as weaving or pottery.

clue.text: Michael. was so'. dynamic!

parts.note: the scientist Michael who discovered electromagnetic induction built the first dynamo, so he was dynamic in a literal sense

explanation.surface: Admiration for a lively man called Michael.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dynamic' means energetic, but here it points to the dynamo: the Victorian physicist Michael who found electromagnetic induction made the first one.
explanation.definitionFit: The English physicist Michael who discovered electromagnetic induction made the first electric generator.

clue.text: " She's of the feminine gender "

parts.note: a grammar-book line about a feminine noun, read instead as a description of a young woman

explanation.surface: A grammar lesson explaining that a noun is feminine.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation reads like a grammar note; the answer is a girl, female by nature rather than by grammar.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl or young woman, especially in Scotland and northern England, is plainly female.

clue.text: It's right always to conclude such a one 'has taken orders

parts.note: ever means always, as in for ever
to end something is to conclude it

explanation.surface: Someone argues it is proper that an ordained person should always finish things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken orders' means ordained into the clergy, not obeyed commands.
explanation.definitionFit: A clergyman, given his title after ordination, is one who has entered holy orders.

clue.text: This show is phenomenal

parts.note: phenomenal is used in its philosophical sense, belonging to what is seen, and a show is an outward look

explanation.surface: A rave review of a stage production.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Phenomenal' reads as a rave, but it means relating to phenomena, the way things look, and 'show' means outward look.
explanation.definitionFit: An outward show is the way something looks, and phenomena are things as they look to us.

clue.text: Unconscious of a huntsman's 'return

indicators.note: a return sends the huntsman's name back the way it came, so read it from the end

parts.note: John Peel is the huntsman of the old hunting song 'D'ye ken John Peel', so his possessive is PEEL'S

explanation.surface: Someone is oblivious to the hunter coming home.
explanation.walkthrough: John Peel was a Cumbrian huntsman celebrated in a well-known English song; 'return' turns PEELS into SLEEP, after A.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in slumber means being out of awareness, dead to the world.

clue.text: It thwarts would-be tea-cup fortune-tellers.

parts.note: fortunes are read from the leaves left in a cup, and a kitchen sieve keeps those leaves out of the cup

explanation.surface: Something spoils the fun of people hoping to read the future in their tea.
explanation.walkthrough: Tea-leaf reading needs leaves in the bottom of the cup; pour through a sieve and there are none to read.
explanation.definitionFit: A sieve held over the cup catches the leaves, leaving the would-be seer nothing to interpret.

clue.text: Beauty 'specialist's main turn, repairing teeth

indicators.note: the turn sends the word for the main backwards

parts.note: the main is an old word for the open sea

indicators.note: repairing means putting the letters of teeth back together in a new order

explanation.surface: A cosmetic dentist takes a sea trip while fixing someone's teeth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beauty specialist' sounds like a beautician or dentist, but it means a connoisseur of beauty; 'turn' makes AES from SEA and 'repairing' makes THETE from TEETH.
explanation.definitionFit: A devotee of art and beauty is someone whose speciality is the beautiful.

clue.text: Harris's brother.

parts.note: Joel Chandler Harris wrote the Uncle Remus tales, where every animal is called by a dialect form of 'brother', as with Rabbit and Fox

explanation.surface: A family note about someone named Harris and his sibling.
explanation.walkthrough: Joel Chandler Harris, an American author, wrote the Uncle Remus stories with characters such as Rabbit and Fox prefixed by a dialect title meaning brother.
explanation.definitionFit: In Harris's Southern dialect stories the title before each creature's name is a clipped form of the word for a male sibling.

clue.text: Put your money on Ham if the track is tricky

parts.note: to back a horse is to put money on it
gammon is a cured ham from the hind leg of a pig

explanation.surface: A tip to bet on a horse called Ham if the racecourse is difficult.
explanation.walkthrough: The racing picture misleads: the board game has a winding track of points round which the pieces race, with tricky blocking play.
explanation.definitionFit: The old board game for two moves pieces round a track of points by dice throws.

clue.text: Low, swinging driver?

parts.note: the spiritual 'Swing Low, Sweet Chariot' is evoked; the person driving such a vehicle is the one meant

explanation.surface: A golfer's drive that swings low.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Driver' and 'swinging' suggest golf, but the words recall the spiritual 'Swing Low, Sweet Chariot', and the driver is whoever handles the chariot.
explanation.definitionFit: The driver of a horse-drawn racing or war vehicle in antiquity held the reins of a chariot.

clue.text: Carried in a fuddled state, beaming all round

indicators.note: a fuddled state is a muddled, drunken condition, so the letters of carried in a are jumbled

explanation.surface: A drunk is carried home, grinning at everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fuddled state' rearranges the letters of CARRIED IN A.
explanation.definitionFit: Light shining out in all directions is radiance spread around.

clue.text: His mate was a clubbable type no doubt

definitions.text: His mate was a clubbable type no doubt

parts.words: His mate was a clubbable type no doubt
parts.note: clubbable normally means sociable, but here it means fit to be hit with a club, as the prehistoric husband of cartoons drags his wife off

explanation.surface: A man's wife was very sociable and good company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clubbable' usually means sociable; read literally it means fit to be clubbed, as in the cartoon image of the Stone Age man dragging his wife by the hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A Stone Age man living in a cave is pictured wielding a club over his mate.

clue.text: Virginia's astride an elk makes: getaway'

indicators.note: astride means the letters for Virginia's sit either side of the animal

parts.note: VA is the abbreviation for the US state of Virginia, plus the S of the possessive
the European elk is the same animal Americans call a moose

explanation.surface: A woman named Virginia sits on an elk and rides off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Astride' puts VA'S on either side of MOOSE.
explanation.definitionFit: The American slang verb for clearing off quickly means to escape or run away.

clue.text: Not like Lucy's: way not even in rent revision

indicators.note: in places the word for not even inside the rearranged letters of rent
a revision reworks the letters of rent into another order

parts.note: a number that is not even is odd

explanation.surface: Someone's habits differ from Lucy's, and the rent review is uneven too.
explanation.walkthrough: Wordsworth's Lucy 'dwelt among the untrodden ways', so not like her ways means well-worn; 'revision' makes TREN of RENT, and 'in' puts ODD inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Wordsworth's Lucy lived where nobody walked, so the opposite is a path much walked upon.

clue.text: Jack's duty — to gaze at Sirius ?

definitions.text: Jack's duty — to gaze at Sirius ?

parts.words: Jack's duty — to gaze at Sirius ?
parts.note: Jack is a sailor, whose short evening shift aboard ship has a name that could mean observing the Dog Star, Sirius

explanation.surface: A sailor on duty looking up at the brightest star in the sky.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack (Jack Tar) is a sailor; the two-hour evening shifts on board are named after the canine, and Sirius is the Dog Star.
explanation.definitionFit: One of the two short evening shifts on a ship, which could be read as keeping an eye on the Dog Star.

clue.text: A singular sight for this giant

definitions.text: A singular sight for this giant

parts.words: A singular sight for this giant
parts.note: singular means remarkable, but also one in number: the giant of Greek myth had just one eye

explanation.surface: Someone describes a remarkable view enjoyed by a huge creature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singular' looks like 'remarkable', but it means single: the one-eyed giant of Homer's Odyssey sees with only one eye.
explanation.definitionFit: The giant of Greek myth blinded by Odysseus had a single eye in his forehead.

clue.text: Is the club, bore so sharp-.. sighted

definitions.text: Is the club, bore so sharp-.. sighted

parts.words: Is the club, bore so sharp-.. sighted
parts.note: a club bore is a tedious member, but a bore is also a boring tool, the small hand drill whose piercing point gives a keen-eyed look its name

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether the dullest member of the club is really so observant.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'bore' is a person who bores, and also a tool for boring holes; the small hand-boring tool, also a gin cocktail served in clubs, gives the adjective for a piercing stare.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyes that seem to drill into things are said to be like a small boring tool, so very keen and observant.

clue.text: What makes Kensington so bloody ?

parts.note: Kensington has a London street whose second word also means spilt blood

explanation.surface: Someone asks why a smart part of London is so violent.
explanation.walkthrough: Kensington Gore is a street in the London district of Kensington, by the Albert Hall; the second word also means clotted blood.
explanation.definitionFit: Spilt or clotted blood is what makes anything bloody, and it completes the Kensington street name.

clue.text: Shylock's gaberdine tailor-made here

indicators.note: made means the letters of tailor are worked into a new form

explanation.surface: The Jewish moneylender's coat was made to measure in this place.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Merchant of Venice Shylock complains that Antonio spat on his 'Jewish gaberdine' on the Rialto, Venice's business quarter; 'made' rearranges TAILOR.
explanation.definitionFit: Shylock says his coat was spat upon on the Rialto, the Venetian exchange where merchants met.

clue.text: Grouse — of. infringement, say, by Othello

parts.note: Shakespeare's Othello is the Moor of Venice

indicators.note: say signals that the word for infringement is pronounced and spelt as its twin

parts.note: a foul is an infringement of the rules in sport

explanation.surface: A complaint about Othello committing an offence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grouse' looks like a verb meaning complain, but it is the bird; 'say' tells you FOUL is heard as FOWL.
explanation.definitionFit: The red grouse is a game bird of the heather uplands, also called by a name for upland birds.

clue.text: Admits a snowdrift

indicators.note: drift means the letters of snow are blown out of place into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to a heap of windblown snow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snowdrift' looks like one word, but 'drift' rearranges SNOW.
explanation.definitionFit: To acknowledge a fault is to confess it as your own.

clue.text: This might perhaps only rate in the baroque style

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the words only rate might be rearranged into something else

explanation.surface: A critic grudgingly gives an ornamented building a modest score.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' rearranges the letters of ONLY RATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Baroque art and architecture are richly decorated, so done in that manner means elaborately adorned.

clue.text: Rome's emperor embraces Bashan's king returning in state

indicators.note: returning turns the whole assembled word back to front
embraces means the emperor's name holds the king's name inside it

parts.note: Nero was a Roman emperor
Og was the giant king of Bashan in the Old Testament

explanation.surface: A Roman ruler hugs a biblical king on his way back into the country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Embraces' puts OG inside NERO to make NOGERO, and 'returning' reads that backwards to give the US state.
explanation.definitionFit: A state of the USA on the Pacific coast, between California and Washington.

clue.text: Doris gets involved -with those of charitable aims for instance

indicators.note: gets involved means the letters of Doris tangle together with the letters of those

explanation.surface: Doris joins a group of people with charitable goals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets involved' mixes DORIS with THOSE.
explanation.definitionFit: A religious or lay community of women is often devoted to charitable work, such as nursing or teaching.
